paragraphs: Friend, this poem is hard to sit through, and it's supposed to be. The poet doesn't hurry past the pain or dress it up. He opens with "How the gold has become tarnished," and he keeps looking at what was lost, one hard picture after another (Lamentations 4:1). Here's what I think that teaches us: God's people are allowed to grieve out loud, and honest sorrow belongs in the Word of God.

The poet also doesn't call it random. He says the LORD poured out His fierce anger (Lamentations 4:11), and he says it was for the sins of the prophets and the priests, who shed the blood of the righteous (Lamentations 4:13). The leaders who were supposed to point people to God did the opposite, and the whole city felt it. So sin is serious, and the people who are supposed to lead others toward God carry a heavy load. Take that one home, baker, and ask the LORD to keep your own heart clean.

But the poem doesn't end in the dark. The poet tells the Daughter of Zion, "your punishment is complete; He will not prolong your exile" (Lamentations 4:22). Even the worst night has an end that God sets. When your gold feels tarnished, baker, hold onto that last line, because God is the One who makes things new (Revelation 21:5), and I'm living proof of what that looks like.
